hook: The old master of the Way, who wrote a little book and rode off into the west.

pages.x: Laozi means "Old Master". Tradition says he kept the royal archives of the Zhou kings in Luoyang in the 6th century BC. Historians are not even sure he existed: the stories about him were written down centuries later, and his book may be the work of many hands.

An old story says the young Confucius came to ask him about ceremonies. Laozi told him to drop his pride and ambition. Afterwards Confucius told his students: "Birds fly, fish swim and beasts run, and I understand them. But the dragon I cannot understand. Today I have met Laozi, and he is like a dragon."
pages.cap: Confucius, who came to learn from him

pages.x: Weary of the decaying Zhou court, Laozi left on the back of a water buffalo. At the Hangu Pass the guard begged him to write down his wisdom before he left the world. Laozi wrote a short book of about 5,000 characters, handed it over, rode on, and was never seen again.

The book, the Tao Te Ching, "The Classic of the Way and its Power", is only 81 short poems. It teaches the Tao, the Way that flows through all things, and wu wei, acting without forcing: "Nothing is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard." It is one of the most translated books in the world.

In later centuries Taoism grew into a religion, with temples, priests and monks, and Laozi was worshipped as a god. The emperors of the Tang dynasty, who shared his family name, Li, claimed him as their ancestor and gave him the title of Supreme Emperor.

With Confucius and the Buddha, Laozi shaped the thought, art and medicine of China. His ideas of balance, simplicity and going with the flow of nature reach far beyond China, and millions still follow Taoism.
pts: Traditional author of the Tao Te Ching
Taught wu wei: acting without forcing
